scenario.name: NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer
scenario.overview: Picture an active industrial factory floor with a moving assembly conveyor belt, an articulated yellow robotic arm, steel parts bins, and a final quality-seal stamping desk. During the quiet night shift on the factory floor, a saboteur steps beside the moving assembly conveyor right before the automated quality stamp. In this real-world scenario, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the factory floor later, then quietly copies a trusted access pass from the factory quality inspector's station. Only when a quality engineer checks the finished product’s weight and internal wiring against the locked master blueprint cabinet does the factory-line swap appear. In this scenario (T1195.001, NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: maintainer Account Takeover, then automatic preinstall Execution, then silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Maintainer Account Takeover, then Automatic preinstall Execution, then Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Maintainer Account Takeover & Malicious preinstall Hook Publish
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1195.001 - Compromise Software Dependencies)
stages.description: During the quiet night shift on the factory floor, a saboteur steps beside the moving assembly conveyor right before the automated quality stamp. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the factory floor later while everyday visitors and the factory quality inspector go about their routine. By compromising maintainer npm credentials that did not enforce two-factor authentication (2FA) for package publishing, the threat actor pushed trojanized versions (ua-parser-js@0.7.29, coa@2.0.3, rc@1.2.9) containing a "preinstall": "node preinstall.js" hook in package.json (an npm lifecycle hook that executes arbitrary shell commands on the host machine automatically before the package is even imported by any application code). Because many upstream libraries declare loose semver ranges (such as ^0.7.0 or ^2.0.0), any developer or CI job running npm install without a strict lockfile automatically pulled the newly published malicious version. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Maintainer Account Takeover & Malicious preinstall Hook Publish / ⇠#1 ALERT T1195.001) from Node ① (#1 Hijacked NPM Account & Payload Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens).

stages.title: Stage 2: Automatic preinstall Execution & curl Download of sdd.dll
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059.007 - JavaScript / T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell)
stages.description: The robotic arm pauses for a heartbeat as the saboteur swaps one genuine component on the belt for an identical-looking counterfeit part carrying a hidden wire. Here in Step 2 inside the factory floor, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the factory quality stamp station in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the original master blueprint cabinet. When npm install ran on a developer workstation, node.exe executed preinstall.js, which fingerprinted the host OS (process.platform) and on Windows spawned cmd.exe /c compile.bat to invoke curl (downloading both an XMRig miner jsextension.exe from 159.148.186.228 and a malicious DLL sdd.dll from citationsheriff.com, saving the DLL locally as create.dll). On Linux workstations and CI containers, the script instead executed preinstall.sh to download and run an ELF cryptominer binary (jsextension). In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc), NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the cmd.exe /c compile.bat request succeeded on NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution & DanaBot Credential Theft). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ cmd.exe /c compile.bat / ⇠#2 ACK 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens).

keySpecs.value: Configure developer workstations with global npm config `ignore-scripts=true` and monitor node.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe during package installation.
Execution (T1059.007 - JavaScript / T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell)

stages.title: Stage 3: Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution & DanaBot Credential Theft
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion & Credential Access (T1218.010 - Regsvr32 / T1555)
stages.description: The assembly line rolls forward, the factory press stamps the official warranty seal right onto the tampered unit, and trucks ship it to every trusting customer. In this final step inside the factory floor, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the factory quality inspector's station until the assembly line inspection camera catches the mismatch. The batch file executed regsvr32.exe -s create.dll (abusing the signed Microsoft COM registration utility with the -s silent flag to invoke the DLL’s DllRegisterServer export without displaying error popups), launching the DanaBot information stealer in memory to harvest saved Chrome/Edge browser passwords, session cookies, Windows DPAPI secrets, SSH private keys, and cloud CLI credentials. Because developers frequently hold privileged AWS, GitHub, and production SSH credentials on their laptops, CISA warned that any workstation that installed these versions had to be treated as fully compromised. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) to Developer Workstation (npm install), Developer Workstation (npm install) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the regsvr32.exe -s create.dll request succeeded on Developer Workstation (npm install) and completing the final execution objective of NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ regsvr32.exe -s create.dll / ⇠#3 ACK 1) from Node ③ (#3 NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc)) to Node ④ (#4 Developer Workstation (npm install)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens).

keySpecs.value: Block regsvr32.exe from loading unsigned DLLs located in user-writable project directories or node_modules folders via WDAC/AppLocker rules.
